## Design

### 2026-10-18 – I wanted a marble run that keeps going on its own, so the marble has to get back to the top somehow. An Archimedes screw seemed like the neatest way to do that, and I’d never built one, so I spent abo

**5h**

I wanted a marble run that keeps going on its own, so the marble has to get back to the top somehow. An Archimedes screw seemed like the neatest way to do that, and I’d never built one, so I spent about 5 hours on a first model in Fusion.

This was my first time using Fusion, so a big chunk of those hours went on just working out where everything is and how it works: the sketches, the timeline, how to revolve and sweep a shape, how to keep each part as its own body. I spent a lot of time clicking around and undoing things before it started to make sense.

The model had a plinko board, a funnel, a round tube for the track, and the screw sitting inside a closed tube with a small motor on top. Getting it all drawn and lined up took a lot longer than I expected. Every part has to hand the marble to the next one at the right height, and I kept finding that my numbers didn’t add up. The lift wasn’t tall enough for the drop it had to make up.

The screw was the real problem. An 8 mm marble is big next to a 14 mm screw on a 4 mm shaft inside a 16 mm tube, and there’s barely any room for it. I couldn’t see a way to make that work on paper, and once I thought about it properly I didn’t trust it. With the tube closed, if the marble wedges between the flights and the wall, you can’t see it or reach it, and the whole machine just stops. The plinko had the same worry: a marble could get stuck in there with no way to get it out.

So I stopped patching it and started again. The next version has an open channel, a screw with a guide rail and nothing around it, and a plinko tray you can see into. If a marble gets stuck now, I can just see it and flick it out.
